7: A consulting firm markets a “decision bootcamp” that trains managers to avoid availability and representativeness shortcuts. Trainers randomly assign half the cohort to spaced retrieval practice on case vignettes and half to a single massed lecture, then compare next-month promotion rates. The firm’s blog claims the bootcamp *caused* better promotions because attendees who later got promoted also scored higher on a post-test of heuristic names. A methods skeptic, a learning theorist, and an HR analyst argue. Which analysis is strongest?

Promotion outcomes are correlational with training exposure; without an intact randomized contrast on promotions and controls for prior performance, causal claims about heuristics training remain weak
Naming availability correctly is itself a classical CS that automatically raises salary via operant extinction of every competing heuristic forever
Massed lecture equals spaced retrieval for long-term transfer, so any promotion gap must be Flynn-effect noise rather than a design problem
Heuristics are phonemes of thought, so only Wernicke’s aphasia studies can validate managerial decision training in this vignette

The design muddles learning schedule effects with uncontrolled promotion criteria; correlating post-test scores with promotions does not prove the bootcamp caused advancement (§7.3; Ch 2 methods; Ch 6 spacing).

7.1: People choosing B confuse labeling a bias with classical conditioning and invent an automatic pay mechanism the vignette never supports.
7.2: People choosing C ignore robust spacing/retrieval advantages and dismiss design flaws as Flynn-effect trivia.
7.3: People choosing D misapply language/brain terms; heuristics are judgment shortcuts, not phonemes, and aphasia is irrelevant here.

7: During a school psych evaluation, Amira’s WISC-like full-scale IQ is average, yet her classroom teacher insists she “must have low g” because she freezes on timed math word problems after noisy cafeteria lunch. The teacher proposes cutting recess to “grow crystallized intelligence.” A neurologist notes recent otitis media may blur speech-in-noise; a cognition tutor suspects working-memory load plus stereotype threat, not a fixed g deficit. Which integration best guides next steps?
Treat the freeze as possible transient sensory/attention load and situational stress interacting with fluid problem solving—not proof of low g or a mandate to cut recess for crystallized gains
g is identical to absolute auditory threshold, so otitis media permanently resets Spearman’s factor and requires recess removal
Crystallized intelligence is stored only in the basilar membrane; recess cuts re-encode semantic memory via cones
Stereotype threat is a positive symptom of schizophrenia, so the WISC should be discarded for a projective inkblot only
IQ composites are not classroom verdicts; sensory noise, working memory, and situational threat can tank timed problem solving without rewriting g (§7.4–7.5; sensation; stress/social).

7.1: People choosing A-confuse (B) equate g with a sensory threshold and invent permanent biological rewriting from ear infection.
7.2: People choosing C scramble sensory anatomy with intelligence theory; crystallized knowledge is not in the cochlea.
7.3: People choosing D pathologize stereotype threat and misuse assessment tools.

7: A quiz app rewards streaks for speed-guessing category exemplars (robin→bird). Users start endorsing weak exemplars (penguin) as non-birds under time pressure, then later “remember” the app taught that penguins are not birds. A product manager calls this insight; a memory researcher smells reconstructive error; a learning analyst sees reinforcement of fast prototype matching. Best cross-topic account?
Operant speed rewards strengthened prototype/heuristic responding, and later recall reconstructed the app’s contingencies as a false semantic rule about penguins
Classical pairing of robin with food pellets extinguished all schemata, proving algorithms never err under time pressure
The misinformation effect requires an eyewitness verb and cannot apply to category learning apps in principle
Phoneme segmentation failure alone explains the penguin endorsement without invoking concepts or reinforcement
Concepts/prototypes guide fast categorization; reinforcement shaped the strategy; memory later distorted the lesson (§7.1; Ch 6; Ch 8).

7.1: People choosing B invent classical food pairing and wrongly claim algorithms are error-free under pressure.
7.2: People choosing C over-restrict misinformation to eyewitness wording; reconstructive memory broader.
7.3: People choosing D reduce a concept/learning issue to speech-sound processing alone.

7: City hall runs a non-randomized “smart streets” campaign after a viral crash video. Planners use the availability of that video to justify expensive redesigns, then point to a post-campaign drop in crashes as proof. Crash counts also fell citywide on untreated roads during a mild winter and reduced nightlife. Stress-team staff report decision-makers felt urgency after sleepless crisis meetings. Strongest critique?
Availability-driven policy plus history/maturation confounds and lacking controls block causal credit to the redesign; stress may bias urgency without fixing internal validity
Any crash decline after a campaign is experimental proof because availability heuristics create random assignment automatically
Mild winter is a positive reinforcer for drivers’ hippocampus, so maturation threats are impossible in traffic data
Sleeplessness raises crystallized intelligence, validating availability-based spending regardless of untreated comparison roads
Salient media (availability) can drive policy, but without controls, history/maturation rival explanations remain (§7.3; Ch 2; stress).

7.1: People choosing B treat post-hoc declines as experiments and invent random assignment from a heuristic.
7.2: People choosing C misuse reinforcement and memory anatomy to deny standard validity threats.
7.3: People choosing D reverse sleep-cognition links and ignore the need for comparison conditions.

7: Parents of a 10-year-old want an IQ retest after a single low group-screening score, fearing fixed low intelligence. The child recently switched schools mid-year (attachment disruption themes), and a parent’s anxiety disorder leads to nightly drilling that the child calls “I’m dumb rehearsals.” A trait psychologist notes high neuroticism in the parent. Best evidence-based framing for the counselor?
One screening score is not a destiny narrative; development, anxiety modeling, and practice conditions can depress performance—reassess with appropriate tests and reduce threat-laden drilling
g is fully set at birth by parental neuroticism scores, so retesting is unethical and drilling must intensify
School switches raise IQ via the Flynn effect within two weeks, so parental anxiety is irrelevant to performance
Attachment disruption converts fluid intelligence into a specific phobia of numbers that only ECT can treat
Intelligence testing needs context; developmental stress and anxiety can suppress scores without proving immutable low g (§7.5; Ch 9; Ch 11/15 themes).

7.1: People choosing B treat g as sealed by a parent’s trait score and prescribe harmful drilling.
7.2: People choosing C misuse the Flynn effect (cohort/generational) as a two-week individual booster.
7.3: People choosing D invent a bizarre fluid-IQ→phobia conversion and jump to ECT inappropriately.

7: A jury hears an expert say defendants “look like typical fraudsters” (representativeness) after a media montage of prior scandals (availability). Defense counsel notes dim courtroom lighting and tired jurors (sensory/attention load). Prosecution claims the heuristic *is* Bayesian rationality. Social psych classmates whisper about persuasion routes. Which statement is most accurate?
Representativeness and availability can bias judgments away from base rates; fatigue and poor viewing conditions further degrade careful systematic processing of evidence
Looking typical is identical to a high d′ in signal detection, so base rates become irrelevant once a prototype matches
Availability from media is classical conditioning of the jury’s optic nerve and therefore legally equivalent to DNA
Central-route persuasion forbids all heuristics, so any mention of prototypes proves juror psychopathology
Heuristics can mislead legal judgment; sensory/cognitive load undermines effortful analysis (§7.3; sensation; social persuasion).

7.1: People choosing B confuse prototype match with perceptual sensitivity (d′) and discard base rates wrongly.
7.2: People choosing C metaphorically abuse classical conditioning and sensory anatomy as legal proof.
7.3: People choosing D overstate ELM: heuristics can still intrude; they are not proof of a disorder.

7: A startup sells “neuroplasticity gum” that supposedly raises triarchic practical intelligence by “coating the hippocampus with crystallized g.” Marketing cites a single correlational survey of gum chewers’ self-rated street smarts. A biopsych intern notes chewing may alter arousal; a memory student asks about encoding vs ability change. Best consumer-science takeaway?
Self-rated correlations plus a biologically implausible mechanism do not validate gum as raising Sternberg-style practical intelligence; arousal or expectancy may explain ratings
Crystallized g is a neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction, so gum chemistry must raise practical intelligence if chewers feel smarter
Triarchic theory equates practical intelligence with flashbulb memory for ads, proving the survey’s causal claim
Any hippocampal mention converts correlational marketing into a true experiment without a control group
Triarchic practical intelligence is not a gum-coated hippocampus; weak correlational self-reports ≠ causal ability gains (§7.4; Ch 2/3/8).

7.1: People choosing B invent a false neurochemical identity for crystallized intelligence.
7.2: People choosing C mash triarchic theory with flashbulb memory and invent causation.
7.3: People choosing D treat anatomical buzzwords as a substitute for experimental control.

7: A language app uses intermittent variable-ratio rewards for translating idioms. Users report “Aha!” moments that feel insightful, then overgeneralize grammar rules (mental set) and ignore counterexamples. Motivation researchers note the streak counter hooks dopamine-like anticipation; emotion researchers note pride labeling after wins. Which account best ties thinking, learning, and motivation?
Variable-ratio reinforcement maintains practice while success-driven affect and mental set can rigidify incorrect grammar generalizations despite counterexamples
Insight moments prove algorithms were used exclusively, so mental set and reinforcement schedules cannot co-occur in language learning
Variable-ratio schedules extinguish all motivation, therefore pride labeling cannot follow streaks in this vignette
Idioms are morphemes stored only in the amygdala, making grammar overgeneralization a drive-reduction event for thirst
Reinforcement sustains engagement; affective labeling and mental set can still produce rigid, wrong rules (§7.2; Ch 6; Ch 10).

7.1: People choosing B treat insight as proof of pure algorithms and deny co-occurring biases/schedules.
7.2: People choosing C reverse how VR schedules typically sustain responding and motivation.
7.3: People choosing D scramble linguistic units with fear anatomy and thirst drives.

8: A podcast host “tests” a memory-boosting playlist by asking callers who already love the songs to free-recall a grocery list after listening, then compares them to silent volunteers recruited from a sleepy late-night chat. Callers recall more and the host declares music *causes* encoding success. Listeners debate attention, levels of processing, and selection. Best critique?
Non-equivalent groups and confounded alertness/preference block causal claims; deeper or more attentive encoding—not the playlist brand—may explain any recall edge
Free recall after music is classical conditioning of the engram, so selection confounds are irrelevant to encoding claims
Silent controls automatically match callers on motivation and circadian state, validating the causal headline
Availability heuristics about catchy intros raise storage capacity of sensory memory from milliseconds to years
Encoding quality and group equivalence matter; the design cannot isolate playlist causation (§8.1–8.2; methods; attention).

8.1: People choosing B misuse classical conditioning language to dismiss basic validity threats.
8.2: People choosing C invent matched controls the vignette never created.
8.3: People choosing D confuse sensory memory duration with judgment heuristics.

8: After a dimly lit store theft, three witnesses watch a news segment saying the suspect “smashed” the case. Later they confidently report broken glass that was never there. A detective trusts confidence as accuracy; a perception student cites poor viewing conditions; a social psychologist cites post-event suggestion. Strongest synthesis?
Low encoding quality plus misleading post-event language can reconstruct memories; confidence is an unreliable accuracy meter under these conditions
Flashbulb vividness from the newscast proves glass existed, because arousal always freezes verbatim sensory traces
Misinformation only alters procedural memory for riding bikes, never episodic reports of crimes
Dim lighting raises absolute thresholds into photographic memory, canceling any suggestion effects
Eyewitness memory is reconstructive; suggestion and poor viewing conditions undermine the confidence–accuracy link (§8.3; sensation; social).

8.1: People choosing B over-trust arousal/flashbulb metaphors as perfect recordings.
8.2: People choosing C mislocate misinformation as only procedural.
8.3: People choosing D invent a sensory upgrade that abolishes suggestion—unsupported.

8: A stroke patient learns a new mirror-tracing skill across days yet cannot declare having practiced (dissociation hinting procedural vs declarative). A PT assistant says dopamine at the NMJ “is the engram.” A behavior tech wants only continuous reinforcement forever. A neuropsych student argues cerebellar/basal-ganglia skill circuits can strengthen without hippocampal declarative report. Best take?
Skill learning can improve via procedural systems without intact episodic report; NMJ dopamine talk confuses motor endplates with memory engrams, and schedule choice should fit therapy goals
If declarative recall fails, procedural learning is impossible by definition in all humans
Continuous reinforcement is required to store any procedural trace because variable schedules erase cerebellum function
Engrams are only semantic capitals of countries, so mirror tracing cannot be remembered in any form
Multiple memory systems allow procedural gains without declarative awareness (§8.2; biopsych; learning).

8.1: People choosing B deny well-documented dissociations between skill and fact memory.
8.2: People choosing C overstate CRF necessity and invent cerebellar erasure by VR schedules.
8.3: People choosing D shrink memory to semantic trivia and ignore motor skill learning.

8: Maya, 78, forgets why she entered rooms and worries she has Alzheimer’s after reading a scary article (availability). Her physician finds sleep debt, new anticholinergic meds, and recent bereavement stress—not progressive aphasia. A grandchild assumes all late-life forgetting is encoding failure of childhood schemas. Best integrated reading?
Normal aging retrieval quirks plus sleep, medication, and stress can mimic alarming forgetting; scary media availability may inflate disease fear without proving neurodegenerative encoding collapse
Bereavement always destroys procedural memory for walking, so room-entry forgetting must be Alzheimer’s
Anticholinergic effects improve LTP forever, proving the article’s causal diagnosis
Childhood schemas cannot be retrieved after age 70 because sensory memory lasts only 30 seconds in older adults exclusively
Differential diagnosis matters: sleep, drugs, stress, and media-fueled availability can amplify worry about memory (§8.4; development; stress).

8.1: People choosing B leap from grief to Alzheimer’s via a false procedural claim.
8.2: People choosing C reverse typical anticholinergic cognitive risks.
8.3: People choosing D misuse sensory-memory duration as an aging law about schemas.

8: Students who self-test with elaborative “why” questions outperform re-readers on a transfer exam, yet a TikTok tip says highlighting is superior because it “feels fluent.” A motivation researcher notes fluency is misattributed ease; a thinking researcher notes recognition vs recall cues. Which conclusion fits best?
Desirable difficulties like retrieval practice often beat fluency illusions from highlighting; feelings of ease are poor metacognitive guides to durable encoding
Fluency during highlighting directly lengthens iconic memory to permanent storage, outperforming any testing effect
Elaborative interrogation only works if paired with a fixed-interval pellet schedule for every why-question
Transfer exams measure phoneme awareness alone, so encoding strategies are irrelevant in this vignette
Metacognitive fluency ≠ learning; retrieval/elaboration typically outperform passive highlighting (§8.1; thinking; motivation/metacognition).

8.1: People choosing B confuse subjective fluency with iconic-memory hardware upgrades.
8.2: People choosing C force an irrelevant operant schedule onto a cognitive strategy finding.
8.3: People choosing D reduce transfer testing to speech sounds alone.

8: After a night of heavy drinking (state-dependent themes) and fragmented sleep, Jordan “recalls” a campus assault detail that first appeared in a friend’s leading text. Counseling staff must avoid implanting further detail while still supporting Jordan. Anxiety is high. Best memory-informed stance?

Treat the report as potentially genuine, reconstructed, or suggested—document carefully, avoid leading probes, and note alcohol/sleep as factors that can distort encoding and retrieval without dismissing distress
State-dependent learning proves the text message detail is verbatim truth because alcohol always improves eyewitness precision
Fragmented sleep creates flashbulb accuracy for suggested events, so leading texts cannot distort memory
Any post-event text automatically means the memory is a delusion requiring antipsychotic medication first-line
Support the person while respecting reconstructive memory and intoxication/sleep effects; do not lead (§8.3; consciousness; clinical caution).

8.1: People choosing B reverse alcohol’s typical impairing effects on encoding.
8.2: People choosing C invent sleep-based immunity to misinformation.
8.3: People choosing D equate possible suggestion with psychosis and jump to meds inappropriately.

8: An airline uses spaced simulator drills (retrieval practice) versus a one-day massed slideshow for emergency checklists. Months later, spaced crews perform better under stress. Management claims “muscle memory tokens” from a token economy caused the gap, though only the spaced group received simulation. Human-factors leads disagree. Best account?
Spacing/retrieval in realistic practice likely drove retention; crediting an unadministered token economy confuses operant buzzwords with the actual training manipulation
Massed slideshows always outperform spaced simulation for procedural checklists under stress
Token economies store episodic memories in iconic sensory registers for months without practice
Stress hormones erase all spacing benefits, so any performance gap must be a Hawthorne lighting effect only
Distributed, retrieval-rich practice explains the advantage; the token story is unsupported here (§8.2; learning; I-O/HF).

8.1: People choosing B contradict typical spacing/simulation advantages for skills.
8.2: People choosing C mash token economies with sensory memory absurdly.
8.3: People choosing D deny spacing benefits and dump the residual into Hawthorne by default.

8: A personality blog claims highly conscientious people never show proactive interference because orderliness “blocks old lists.” Evidence offered: a tiny convenience sample correlating conscientiousness with self-reported “never forgetting.” A lab instead finds standard PI in paired-associate tasks regardless of Big Five scores. Best methods-plus-memory conclusion?
Self-report correlations on convenience samples cannot overturn controlled PI findings; conscientiousness is not an immunity certificate against interference
Proactive interference cannot occur in laboratory paired-associate tasks by definition
Big Five facets are encoding strategies, so any correlation proves causation of memory immunity
Convenience samples are true random experiments when the dependent variable is forgetting
PI is a robust laboratory memory effect; weak personality self-report links don’t erase it (§8.4; methods; personality).

8.1: People choosing B deny a classic, well-replicated interference phenomenon.
8.2: People choosing C conflate traits with strategies and correlation with causation.
8.3: People choosing D redefine convenience sampling as randomization.
